# GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Security Hub, Detective, Config and Artifact: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=detection-q008 -->
### Question 1

A company has used Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub CSPM, and Amazon Detective in all its accounts for a year. GuardDuty reports that an IAM role made API calls that are unusual for the role. A security engineer must determine the root cause. The engineer needs to see which IP addresses the role used during the past weeks and which API calls the role made. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

- Open the finding in AWS Security Hub CSPM, and create an insight that groups the related findings of the role.
- Query the AWS CloudTrail logs in Amazon S3 with Amazon Athena, and write queries that group the role's calls by source IP address.
- Pivot from the GuardDuty finding into Amazon Detective, and review the activity of the role in the behavior graph.
- Create a GuardDuty suppression rule for the finding type, and review the archived findings of the role.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Pivot from the GuardDuty finding into Amazon Detective, and review the activity of the role in the behavior graph.

**Deciding phrases.** "determine the root cause", "which IP addresses the role used during the past weeks", "LEAST development effort"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST development effort.
2. I mark the constraints: the finding already exists, the engineer needs its root cause, and the engineer must see the role's IP addresses and API calls over the past weeks. Detective has run for a year, so its data covers that time.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict Amazon Detective, because it investigates an existing finding, and its behavior graph already holds CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow Logs and GuardDuty findings.
4. I remove the suppression rule, because GuardDuty still generates the findings and archiving explains nothing. I remove the Security Hub insight, because it groups findings but does not trace the activity of one role.
5. Between Detective and the Athena queries the difference is the code; the stem says LEAST development effort, so I choose Detective, where I write no queries.
6. Check: Detective shows the IP addresses and API calls of the role over time, and I pivot to it from the finding. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** The finding exists; the engineer needs its cause. Detective helps [quickly identify the root cause of security findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-definition-root-cause) from collected log data. Its behavior graph uses [CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow logs, and GuardDuty findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-core-sources), so the IP addresses and API calls of the role are already there, and the engineer writes no queries.

**Why not.**

- "Open the finding in AWS Security Hub CSPM, ...": Security Hub [aggregates, organizes, and prioritizes your security alerts](../facts/detective.md#detective-vs-guardduty-vs-security-hub); grouping findings does not trace the IP addresses and API calls behind one finding.
- "Query the AWS CloudTrail logs in Amazon S3 ...": It can work, but the engineer writes and tunes queries; with Detective you do not [develop, configure, or tune your own queries](../facts/detective.md#detective-no-queries-to-build).
- "Create a GuardDuty suppression rule for the finding ...": A suppression rule archives matching findings, and [GuardDuty still generates all findings](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-suppression-rule-still-generates); archiving explains nothing about the cause.

**Twin.** If the stem said "keep the findings from every account in one prioritized list" instead: AWS Security Hub, because it [aggregates, organizes, and prioritizes your security alerts](../facts/detective.md#detective-vs-guardduty-vs-security-hub).

**Takeaway.** Root cause of one finding without writing queries: Amazon Detective.

**Review.** [Security Hub gathers findings in one place and Detective traces their cause](2-deep.md#security-hub-gathers-findings-in-one-place-and-detective-traces-their-cause-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in many AWS accounts. The accounts belong to one organization in AWS Organizations. The security team works from one dedicated security account and wants to manage the solution for all member accounts from there. The security team must receive an alert when an instance communicates with IP addresses that are known to be malicious. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Enable Amazon GuardDuty for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.
- Activate Amazon Inspector for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.
- Enable Amazon Detective for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.
- Install an open-source security agent on every instance, send its output to an Amazon S3 bucket, and review the results in the security account.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Enable Amazon GuardDuty for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.

**Deciding phrases.** "communicates with IP addresses that are known to be malicious", "all member accounts", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Traffic to a known malicious IP address is activity, and activity is what GuardDuty watches. GuardDuty uses [threat intelligence feeds](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-uses-threat-intel-and-ml) to spot it. [The delegated GuardDuty administrator account](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-delegated-admin-organizations) manages the member accounts, and [you don't need to enable anything else](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-foundational-nothing-else-to-enable) for the foundational data sources.

**Why not.**

- "Activate Amazon Inspector for every account in the ...": Inspector scans workloads for [software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-dg-vulnerabilities-exposure), not for traffic to known malicious IP addresses.
- "Enable Amazon Detective for every account in the ...": Detective [simplifies the process of investigating security findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-vs-guardduty-vs-security-hub); the service that watches for malicious activity is GuardDuty.
- "Install an open-source security agent on every instance, ...": It can work, but the team installs and updates agents on every instance; GuardDuty instead [pulls independent data streams directly](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-faq-no-need-to-enable-source-logs).

**Twin.** If the stem said "runs a software package that has a published common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVE) entry" instead: Amazon Inspector, because it scans for [software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-dg-vulnerabilities-exposure).

**Takeaway.** Traffic to a known malicious IP address is activity: GuardDuty. A vulnerable package is software: Inspector.

**Review.** [GuardDuty analyzes its own copy of your logs and stores none of them](2-deep.md#guardduty-analyzes-its-own-copy-of-your-logs-and-stores-none-of-them-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company stores call transcripts as text objects in many Amazon S3 buckets across several AWS accounts. Some transcripts contain sensitive data such as credit card numbers. Auditors require the company to identify which objects contain credit card numbers. The check must run again every day so that it also covers the transcripts that arrive after the first check. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Enable Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection in the accounts, and review the findings that it generates for the buckets that hold the transcripts.
- Write an AWS Lambda function that runs a regular expression for card numbers on every object each day, and store the matches in a table.
- Create an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job for the buckets that runs daily and uses the managed data identifiers for card numbers.
- Create an AWS Config rule that checks that default encryption is turned on for every bucket, and review the buckets that are noncompliant.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job for the buckets that runs daily and uses the managed data identifiers for card numbers.

**Deciding phrases.** "identify which objects contain credit card numbers", "run again every day", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Card numbers inside objects are sensitive data in Amazon S3, and Macie [discovers sensitive data by using machine learning](../facts/macie.md#macie-dg-discovers-sensitive-data) and pattern matching. A sensitive data discovery job gives [deeper, more targeted analysis](../facts/macie.md#macie-discovery-jobs-targeted) of the buckets that you choose, and a job that runs [on a recurring basis for periodic analysis](../facts/macie.md#macie-discovery-jobs-targeted), such as daily, covers new transcripts without code.

**Why not.**

- "Enable Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection in the accounts, ...": S3 Protection monitors [AWS CloudTrail data events for Amazon S3](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-s3-protection-data-events) to find threats such as data exfiltration, not card numbers inside objects.
- "Write an AWS Lambda function that runs a ...": It can work, but the team writes and maintains the code; Macie managed data identifiers already detect [credit card numbers and bank account numbers](../facts/macie.md#macie-managed-data-identifiers).
- "Create an AWS Config rule that checks that ...": A Config rule [represents desired configurations for a resource](../facts/config.md#config-faq-rule-desired-configuration), such as bucket encryption; a bucket setting does not show which objects hold card numbers.

**Twin.** If the stem said "scan each new transcript for malware when it is uploaded" instead: GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3, because [GuardDuty automatically starts a malware scan](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-malware-s3-scans-new-uploads) on each upload.

**Takeaway.** Card numbers or PII inside S3 objects point to Macie; threats against S3 point to GuardDuty.

**Review.** [Macie samples S3 objects for sensitive data and reports exposed buckets](2-deep.md#macie-samples-s3-objects-for-sensitive-data-and-reports-exposed-buckets-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs a payment application on AWS. As part of an annual audit, an external auditor asks the company for the AWS SOC 2 report and the AWS PCI DSS attestation of compliance. The auditor will use these documents to assess the controls of the AWS data centers and services that the application uses. The auditor reviews the company's own controls separately. What should a solutions architect do to provide these documents?

- Enable the PCI DSS standard in AWS Security Hub CSPM, and export the control findings for the auditor.
- Download the documents from AWS Artifact in the AWS Management Console, and send them to the auditor.
- Deploy an AWS Config conformance pack for PCI DSS in every account, and send the compliance results to the auditor.
- Run Amazon Inspector CIS scans on all Amazon EC2 instances, and send the scan reports to the auditor.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Download the documents from AWS Artifact in the AWS Management Console, and send them to the auditor.

**Deciding phrases.** "the AWS SOC 2 report", "assess the controls of the AWS data centers and services"

**Why.** The auditor asks for reports that AWS writes about the AWS side. AWS Artifact gives [on-demand downloads of AWS security and compliance documents](../facts/artifact.md#artifact-guide-on-demand-compliance-documents), such as [System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports](../facts/artifact.md#artifact-guide-on-demand-compliance-documents). These documents show [the security and compliance of the AWS infrastructure](../facts/artifact.md#artifact-guide-audit-artifacts-for-auditors); the company proves its own controls with its own evidence.

**Why not.**

- "Enable the PCI DSS standard in AWS Security ...": CSPM controls check the company's own resources, and its standards [don't guarantee compliance with any regulatory frameworks](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-no-compliance-guarantee); they are not AWS reports.
- "Deploy an AWS Config conformance pack for PCI ...": A conformance pack holds [AWS Config rules and remediation actions](../facts/config.md#config-guide-conformance-pack) that check the company's own resources, not the AWS data centers.
- "Run Amazon Inspector CIS scans on all Amazon ...": CIS scans [benchmark your Amazon EC2 instance operating systems](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-cis-scans), which belong to the company, so the result is not an AWS audit report.

**Twin.** If the stem said "evidence that the company's own resources follow PCI DSS" instead: the PCI DSS standard in Security Hub CSPM, because a standard is [a set of requirements](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-standard-definition) checked against the company's resources.

**Takeaway.** AWS SOC and PCI reports about AWS itself come from AWS Artifact, not from checks of your resources.

**Review.** [Artifact gives the AWS side of an audit and you keep your own evidence](2-deep.md#artifact-gives-the-aws-side-of-an-audit-and-you-keep-your-own-evidence-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company has recorded the configuration of its resources with AWS Config in all its accounts and Regions for the past year. During an audit, an auditor asks which inbound rules one specific security group had at a point in time three months ago. Engineers have changed the security group several times since then. Which AWS service or feature should a solutions architect use to answer the auditor's question?

- Review the AWS CloudTrail event history for the security group to see its inbound rules on that date.
- Review the Amazon GuardDuty findings of the account to see the inbound rules of the security group on that date.
- Review the AWS Security Hub CSPM security score of the account to see the inbound rules of the security group on that date.
- Review the configuration history of the security group in AWS Config to see its configuration item for that date.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Review the configuration history of the security group in AWS Config to see its configuration item for that date.

**Deciding phrases.** "inbound rules one specific security group had at a point in time", "recorded the configuration of its resources"

**Why.** The auditor asks what the security group looked like, not who changed it. AWS Config keeps a [resource inventory, configuration history, and configuration change notifications](../facts/config.md#config-faq-what-it-is). Because Config was recording, its history shows [the port rules that were open](../facts/config.md#config-guide-security-analysis-history) on the date that the auditor names.

**Why not.**

- "Review the AWS CloudTrail event history for the ...": CloudTrail answers [who made an API call](../facts/config.md#config-faq-vs-cloudtrail) that changed the group; the auditor asks what the group looked like on one date.
- "Review the Amazon GuardDuty findings of the account ...": GuardDuty [continuously monitors your AWS accounts, workloads, runtime activity](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-dg-continuous-malicious-activity) for malicious activity; its findings are not a history of security group rules.
- "Review the AWS Security Hub CSPM security score ...": CSPM uses the results of its checks [to calculate security scores](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-security-score); a score is a summary, not a record of past rules.

**Twin.** If the stem said "which engineer changed the inbound rules" instead: AWS CloudTrail, because it [records user API activity on your account](../facts/config.md#config-faq-cloudtrail-records-api-activity) with the identity of the caller.

**Takeaway.** What a resource looked like at a past time: AWS Config. Who changed it: AWS CloudTrail.

**Review.** [Config judges a change against your rules after the change is recorded](2-deep.md#config-judges-a-change-against-your-rules-after-the-change-is-recorded-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances in many AWS accounts. The accounts belong to one organization in AWS Organizations. The security team works from one dedicated security account and wants to manage the solution for all member accounts from there. The security team must receive an alert when an instance runs a software package that has a published common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVE) entry. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Enable Amazon GuardDuty for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.
- Activate Amazon Inspector for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.
- Enable Amazon Detective for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.
- Install an open-source security agent on every instance, send its output to an Amazon S3 bucket, and review the results in the security account.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Activate Amazon Inspector for every account in the organization through a delegated administrator, and review the results in the security account.

**Deciding phrases.** "runs a software package that has a published common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVE) entry", "all member accounts", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** A package with a published CVE is a weakness in software, and software is what Inspector scans. With Inspector you [don't need to manually schedule or configure](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-no-scheduled-assessments) assessment scans: it rescans after a new CVE is published. [The delegated administrator account for Amazon Inspector](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-delegated-admin-organizations) manages the whole organization from the security account.

**Why not.**

- "Enable Amazon GuardDuty for every account in the ...": GuardDuty [continuously monitors your AWS accounts, workloads, runtime activity](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-dg-continuous-malicious-activity) for malicious activity; a vulnerable package is a weakness in software, not activity.
- "Enable Amazon Detective for every account in the ...": Detective helps [identify the root cause of security findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-dg-root-cause); scanning the packages of an instance for CVEs is the job of Inspector.
- "Install an open-source security agent on every instance, ...": It can work, but the team installs and patches an agent on every instance; Amazon Inspector is activated [for your entire organization with a single click](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-delegated-admin-organizations).

**Twin.** If the stem said "communicates with IP addresses that are known to be malicious" instead: Amazon GuardDuty, because it uses [lists of malicious IP addresses and domains](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-uses-threat-intel-and-ml).

**Takeaway.** A vulnerable package is software: Inspector. Traffic to a known malicious IP address is activity: GuardDuty.

**Review.** [Inspector rescans a workload when a new vulnerability is published](2-deep.md#inspector-rescans-a-workload-when-a-new-vulnerability-is-published-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company uses AWS Organizations with all features enabled. Administrators in member accounts have full permissions in their own accounts. The company must ensure that no one in a member account, including the root user, can turn off S3 Block Public Access at the account level. The company must also find every S3 bucket that has server access logging turned off, including buckets that already have it off today, and must turn logging back on automatically. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies the action that changes the account-level S3 Block Public Access settings.
- Create an AWS Config rule in proactive mode that blocks any change to the account-level S3 Block Public Access settings.
- Write an AWS Lambda function that runs every hour, checks the logging setting of every bucket, and turns logging on where it is off.
- Create an AWS Config rule that checks server access logging on each bucket, with automatic remediation through a Systems Manager Automation document.
- Enable Amazon GuardDuty in every member account, and use an Amazon EventBridge rule to turn logging back on when a finding arrives.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Attach an SCP to the organization root that denies the action that changes the account-level S3 Block Public Access settings.
- Create an AWS Config rule that checks server access logging on each bucket, with automatic remediation through a Systems Manager Automation document.

**Deciding phrases.** "including the root user", "including buckets that already have it off today", "turn logging back on automatically", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The stem has two needs. Prevention against administrators and the root user needs an SCP, because [AWS Config rules do not prevent the user](../facts/config.md#config-faq-rules-evaluate-after-change-not-prevent) from making a change. Detection and repair of a bucket setting is a Config rule with [AWS Systems Manager Automation documents](../facts/config.md#config-guide-remediation-ssm-automation) as automatic remediation.

- The SCP applies [including the member account's root user](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-applies-to-member-root-user), and member principals [cannot remove or change SCPs that are applied to that account](../facts/iam.md#iam-scp-faq-member-principals-cannot-change-scps).
- The rule [flags the resource as noncompliant](../facts/config.md#config-guide-rules-flag-noncompliant), detective rules [evaluate resources that have already been deployed](../facts/config.md#config-guide-proactive-vs-detective), and [you can either choose manual or automatic remediation](../facts/config.md#config-guide-remediation-ssm-automation).

**Why not.**

- "Create an AWS Config rule in proactive mode ...": Proactive rules evaluate resources before deployment, but [proactive rules do not remediate resources](../facts/config.md#config-guide-proactive-vs-detective) or stop their deployment.
- "Write an AWS Lambda function that runs every ...": It can work, but the team writes and runs code on a schedule; AWS Config offers [a set of managed automation documents](../facts/config.md#config-guide-remediation-ssm-automation) for remediation.
- "Enable Amazon GuardDuty in every member account, and ...": GuardDuty analyzes events such as [AWS CloudTrail management events](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-foundational-sources-list), so it reports logging being turned off; it does not check buckets that already had logging off.

**Twin.** If the stem said "alert the team when an administrator turns off S3 Block Public Access" instead: an AWS Config rule alone, because a rule [flags the resource as noncompliant](../facts/config.md#config-guide-rules-flag-noncompliant) after the change.

**Takeaway.** Stop a change for everyone in member accounts with an SCP; find and fix drift with a Config rule and remediation.

**Review.** [Config judges a change against your rules after the change is recorded](2-deep.md#config-judges-a-change-against-your-rules-after-the-change-is-recorded-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A startup runs Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS account and one AWS Region. The account has no AWS CloudTrail trail and no VPC flow logs. The startup needs to detect compromised instances and the use of stolen credentials as soon as possible. The startup wants a fully managed service and has no security engineers to tune detection logic. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Enable Amazon GuardDuty in the Region, and review the findings that it generates from its foundational data sources.
- Turn on VPC flow logs, DNS query logging, and a CloudTrail trail first, and then enable Amazon GuardDuty in the Region.
- Send VPC flow logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and create metric filters and alarms for traffic patterns that suggest a compromised instance.
- Activate Amazon Inspector in the Region, and use its network reachability scans to find the instances that are compromised.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Enable Amazon GuardDuty in the Region, and review the findings that it generates from its foundational data sources.

**Deciding phrases.** "no AWS CloudTrail trail and no VPC flow logs", "compromised instances and the use of stolen credentials", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** GuardDuty reads [AWS CloudTrail management events](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-foundational-sources-list), VPC flow logs and DNS logs through its own streams. [You don't need to enable anything else](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-foundational-nothing-else-to-enable) for these foundational sources, and GuardDuty [does not affect any of your existing](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-flow-logs-not-required) flow logs configuration. Its findings include instance compromise and account compromise.

**Why not.**

- "Turn on VPC flow logs, DNS query logging, ...": It works, but the extra steps add nothing for GuardDuty: [you don't need to create or configure](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-flow-logs-not-required) VPC flow logs for it.
- "Send VPC flow logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, ...": The team writes and tunes every filter, and flow logs hold no API calls; GuardDuty brings [threat intelligence feeds](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-uses-threat-intel-and-ml) and machine learning models.
- "Activate Amazon Inspector in the Region, and use ...": Inspector finds [network reachability issues](../facts/inspector.md#inspector-ec2-network-reachability) and vulnerable packages; these are weaknesses, not an instance or credential that is already in use by an attacker.

**Twin.** If the stem said "keep the network logs for one year for later analysis" instead: turn on VPC flow logs to Amazon S3, because [GuardDuty does not manage or retain your logs](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-does-not-retain-logs).

**Takeaway.** GuardDuty needs no trail or flow logs from you: enable it, and it reads its own streams.

**Review.** [GuardDuty analyzes its own copy of your logs and stores none of them](2-deep.md#guardduty-analyzes-its-own-copy-of-your-logs-and-stores-none-of-them-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company lets customers upload documents to an Amazon S3 bucket through a web application. The company must scan each newly uploaded object for malware before other systems process the object. The company must also find personally identifiable information (PII) in the objects that the bucket stores. The company prefers fully managed AWS services. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Enable Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 on the upload bucket, and use the scan result to decide which objects to process.
- Enable Amazon Macie for the account, and configure Macie to scan each newly uploaded object in the bucket for malware.
- Enable Amazon Detective for the account, and use its behavior graph to find malware and PII in the uploaded objects.
- Enable Amazon Macie, and run a sensitive data discovery job on the bucket that uses managed data identifiers for PII.
- Create an AWS Lambda function that runs an open-source antivirus engine on each upload, and update its virus definitions every day.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Enable Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 on the upload bucket, and use the scan result to decide which objects to process.
- Enable Amazon Macie, and run a sensitive data discovery job on the bucket that uses managed data identifiers for PII.

**Deciding phrases.** "scan each newly uploaded object for malware", "find personally identifiable information (PII)", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The stem has two needs. Malware in each new upload is a GuardDuty job: Malware Protection for S3 scans [newly uploaded objects](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-malware-s3-scans-new-uploads-managed) in the buckets that you select. PII in stored objects is a Macie job, because Macie is a [fully managed sensitive data discovery service](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-faq-vs-macie).

- [GuardDuty automatically starts a malware scan](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-malware-s3-scans-new-uploads) when an object is uploaded to the selected bucket, with no scanning engine to run.
- Macie managed data identifiers detect [personally identifiable information (PII)](../facts/macie.md#macie-managed-data-identifiers) such as passport numbers in S3 objects.

**Why not.**

- "Enable Amazon Macie for the account, and configure ...": Macie [discovers sensitive data by using machine learning](../facts/macie.md#macie-dg-discovers-sensitive-data); malware in new uploads is the job of GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3.
- "Enable Amazon Detective for the account, and use ...": The behavior graph is built from [CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow logs, and GuardDuty findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-core-sources), not from the content of objects.
- "Create an AWS Lambda function that runs an ...": It can work, but the team packages, runs and updates the engine; Malware Protection for S3 scans [newly uploaded objects](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-malware-s3-scans-new-uploads-managed) as a managed feature.

**Twin.** If the stem said "detect unusual API calls that read many objects from the bucket" instead: GuardDuty S3 Protection, because it monitors [AWS CloudTrail data events for Amazon S3](../facts/guardduty.md#guardduty-s3-protection-data-events).

**Takeaway.** Malware in new S3 uploads: GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3. Sensitive data in stored objects: Macie.

**Review.** [Macie samples S3 objects for sensitive data and reports exposed buckets](2-deep.md#macie-samples-s3-objects-for-sensitive-data-and-reports-exposed-buckets-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 10

A company uses AWS Security Hub CSPM in us-east-1 and us-west-2 for all accounts of its organization. The company has not enabled the new AWS Security Hub. The AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard is enabled in both Regions. Control findings appear for resources in us-east-1, but none appear for resources in us-west-2. The company currently records resource configurations with AWS Config in us-east-1 only. Which solution will produce the missing control findings with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Configure cross-Region aggregation with us-east-1 as the home Region and us-west-2 as a linked Region, so that the checks start in us-west-2.
- Write AWS Lambda functions in us-west-2 that check each resource against the standard and import the results into Security Hub CSPM as findings.
- Enable AWS Config in us-west-2 for every account in the organization, and record the resources that the controls of the standard check.
- Enable Amazon Detective in us-west-2 for every account in the organization, and turn on its source package for Security Hub CSPM data.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Enable AWS Config in us-west-2 for every account in the organization, and record the resources that the controls of the standard check.

**Deciding phrases.** "Control findings appear for resources in us-east-1, but none appear for resources in us-west-2", "AWS Config in us-east-1 only", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The standard is enabled in us-west-2, but most of its checks run on AWS Config. Security Hub CSPM [uses service-linked rules from AWS Config](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-uses-config-rules) for most controls, and [you must enable AWS Config and record resources](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-uses-config-rules) to get those control findings. Turning on Config with resource recording in us-west-2 for every account lets the existing controls produce findings.

**Why not.**

- "Configure cross-Region aggregation with us-east-1 as the home ...": Aggregation brings findings that already exist [to a single home Region](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-cross-region-aggregation); it does not create control findings that AWS Config never evaluated.
- "Write AWS Lambda functions in us-west-2 that check ...": It can work, but the team writes and maintains checks that the standard already has; CSPM runs them itself after AWS Config records the resources.
- "Enable Amazon Detective in us-west-2 for every account ...": Detective [simplifies the process of investigating security findings](../facts/detective.md#detective-vs-guardduty-vs-security-hub); it reads findings and creates no control findings for a standard.

**Twin.** If the stem said "control findings appear in both Regions, but the team must review them from us-east-1" instead: cross-Region aggregation, because it brings findings [to a single home Region](../facts/security-hub.md#security-hub-cspm-cross-region-aggregation).

**Takeaway.** Security Hub CSPM control findings need AWS Config recording in every Region and account where CSPM runs.

**Review.** [Security Hub gathers findings in one place and Detective traces their cause](2-deep.md#security-hub-gathers-findings-in-one-place-and-detective-traces-their-cause-5-min)

</details>
